To form the futuro simple: hablaré, comerás, vivirá.
To use the 12 irregular verbs: tendré, haré, podré, saldré…

To express probability: Estará en casa (he’s probably at home).

The future is stressed on the last syllable (except nosotros): habla-RÉ, come-RÁS, vivi-RÁ. Nosotros: habla-RE-mos.
The irregulars have consonant clusters: ten-DRÉ, sal-DRÉ, ven-DRÉ, po-DRÉ. Pronounce the “dr” clearly.
“si” without an accent = if; “sí” with an accent = yes. In speech, “sí” is stressed more.
1. The futuro simple: the easiest tense
The good news: you DON’T cut off the ending! You add the same endings directly to the infinitive (hablar, comer, vivir) for every verb:
The endings look like the verb HABER in the present (he, has, ha, hemos…). That’s no coincidence: historically, “hablaré” = “hablar he” (I have to speak).
Only the stem changes; the endings stay the same (-é, -ás, -á…).
poder → podr-, saber → sabr-, querer → querr-, haber → habr-
tener → tendr-, poner → pondr-, salir → saldr-, venir → vendr-
“Habrá” = the future of “hay”: Mañana habrá una fiesta = There will be a party tomorrow.
3. Ir a + infinitive or the futuro?
You already have a future from chapter 12 (“voy a viajar”). When do you use which?
Esta noche voy a cenar con Ana.
In ordinary conversation, Spaniards use “ir a” more often — a bit like English “going to” versus “will”. The futuro sounds more “serious” or distant.
4. The real condition: SI + present → future
For “if… then…” (something possible), after SI you use the PRESENT, not the future — exactly like English: “If it rains, I’ll stay at home.”
If we save, we’ll go to Japan.
If it rains, I won’t go out.
The classic mistake: “Si lloverá, no saldré”. Never put the future after SI (just as you don’t say “if it will rain” in English)!
A very Spanish trick: the futuro can express a guess about the PRESENT. It’s like English “he’ll be…” or “he must be…”.
Where’s Kenji? — He’ll be at the restaurant. (probably)
What time is it? — It must be about five.
Other ways to express uncertainty: quizás / tal vez (maybe), seguramente (probably), a lo mejor (maybe).
“If I have time, I’ll call you.”
In two years I’ll speak Spanish very well.

In Spanish class, Ana gave her students a special exercise: to write a letter to themselves in fifteen years’ time.
To give them an example, she wrote her own.
“Dear Ana of the year 2040: today you are forty-seven. What will you be like? Where will you live?”
“I think you’ll still be in Madrid, because you can’t live far from your family and the sun.”
“But maybe you’ll spend your summers in Romania, in a house in the mountains.”
“I imagine you’ll be married to Mihai. You’ll have two children, or three, and a big dog called Cocido.”
“Your children will speak Spanish, Romanian and English. And they’ll surely speak Japanese better than you, thanks to Uncle Kenji.”
“At work, I hope you’ll still be teaching. Maybe you’ll have your own language school.”
“There will be robots and automatic translators, but people will still want to learn languages with a real person.”
“Grandma Rosario will be ninety-five. She’ll still be making cocido on Sundays and still be beating everyone at cards.”
“Future Ana, I ask you three things.”
“First: you won’t work too much. Second: you’ll travel to a new country at least once a year.”
“And third: you’ll never stop reading novels on the metro, even if you have a car.”
“If you read this letter in 2040 and everything is different, that’s fine. What matters is that you’re happy. A hug from today’s Ana.”
When she finished reading it, her students applauded. And they started writing.
Ana put her letter in an envelope and wrote: “Do not open until 2040”. Then she put the envelope in her memory box, next to her childhood photos.
Mihai saw it and asked her what it was. “It’s a secret,” she answered. “You’ll find out in fifteen years.”
“nunca dejarás de” = you will never stop
